sections.text: Kurdish cooking comes from the mountains: wheat and bulgur, lamb, yoghurt and plenty of herbs. Rice appears as a side or as a filling, and chickpeas and lentils go into soups and stews. Seasoning comes from sumac, mint, isot pepper and pomegranate molasses, sweetness from dims, the boiled-down grape syrup.

sections.heading: Bread and the winter store
sections.text: Bread is baked thin, on the domed griddle as nanê sêlê or in the clay oven as nanê tenûrê. Much of the cooking is meant for winter: qawirme is lamb preserved in its own fat, kurût are dried yoghurt balls, and aubergines and peppers are dried for winter dolma.

sections.heading: Soups with yoghurt
sections.text: Yoghurt soups are among the most typical dishes. Dokliw is cooked with broken rice, doxewa with rice, chickpeas and herbs, germiya dew with wheat and mint. For weddings there is doğava with meat and small meatballs.

sections.heading: Stuffed and braised
sections.text: Almost everything gets stuffed: vine leaves as îprax, cabbage as dolmê kelemê, chard as pelpêç. Then there are braised lamb dishes, such as bamye with okra, alûcîye with plums, or beh bi goşt with quinces and lentils.

sections.heading: Feasts and sweets
sections.text: For Newroz and Eid people bake: kade, kulîçe with dates and walnuts, nanê birincî made from rice flour. Sweets rely on grape syrup and walnuts, as in helaw, hesîde or bastêq, the grape leather.
